title: Uncertainty-Aware Estimation of Mis/Disinformation Prevalence on Social Media (arXiv 2603.11058)
screen_reason: A dedicated prevalence study: 11,835 social-media posts from six platforms in four EU countries, view-weighted-sampled from a fact-checker-curated keyword corpus and labelled by professional fact-checkers, with the share labelled mis/disinformation reported by language, by platform and by platform-language under two denominator definitions. These are shares of items in a sample classified false or misleading, i.e. CONTENT estimates, and are reported with denominators. Clear INCLUDE.

estimates.country: France (reported as the French-language subsample; the study covers four EU Member States, one language each)
estimates.platform: Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, TikTok, X/Twitter and YouTube pooled
estimates.date: 17 March to 13 April 2025 (data collection); abstract states "between March and April 2025"
estimates.measure_type: % of annotated French-language social-media posts (view-weighted sample, six platforms pooled) labelled mis/disinformation, among posts judged mis/disinformation, credible or unverifiable (P_restricted, baseline)
estimates.denominator: The French-language posts labelled Mis/disinformation, Credible and informative or Unverifiable, out of 2,947 annotated French-language posts (view-weighted random sample of 500 posts per platform per country, six platforms)
estimates.definition: Post labelled Mis/disinformation, divided by the posts labelled Mis/disinformation + Credible and informative + Unverifiable (P_restricted, Equation 2 - the paper's primary definition; posts labelled Borderline, Abusive, Irrelevant, Other language, Deleted or Don't know are excluded from BOTH numerator and denominator).
estimates.misinfo_def: "Mis/disinformation: Content stating or clearly implying a verifiably false or misleading claim that may cause public harm." (Table 1). The study deliberately merges misinformation and disinformation: "we do not differentiate between misinformation (i.e., false or misleading information shared unintentionally) and disinformation (where intention to deceive is present), as both might cause harm"; the Code of Conduct definition it starts from is "verifiably false or misleading information that is created, presented, and disseminated for economic gain or to intentionally deceive the public, and that may cause public harm".
estimates.n: subset of 2,947 annotated French-language posts (the restricted denominator itself is not reported as a count)
estimates.page_loc: Table 2 and Section 4.1 'Per Language Results', p. 15-16
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Professional fact-checkers (SIMODS project, Science Feedback). A Junior fact-checker annotated the full sample of 3,000 posts per language against a nine-category codebook refined in pilot tests; a Senior fact-checker independently re-annotated a random 20% subset (600 posts per language, 581-595 after removing posts labelled Deleted), and disagreements in that double-coded subset were resolved by discussion into a final agreed label. NO inter-coder agreement statistic (kappa or percent agreement) is reported anywhere; instead disagreement is modelled as a 3x3 Junior-to-agreed transition matrix and propagated to the Junior-only remainder by multinomial simulation.
estimates.moderator_quote: To approximate the information environment that users encounter online, a multilingual corpus was constructed using approximately 100 curated keywords per language covering five major topical domains, i.e., the Russo-Ukrainian conflict, climate change, health (including COVID-19), migration, and local politics. Keyword lists were developed and validated by professional fact-checkers to balance neutral keywords (representing about 50%) with ambiguous and misinformation-related terms representing the other half of the keywords. ... To ensure the annotated data reflected the content with the greatest audience reach, a view-weighted random sample of 500 posts per platform for each country (N = 3,000) was retrieved. This approach ensures that the probability of a post being selected is proportional to its number of views, thereby prioritising content with higher visibility in the corpus.
estimates.notes: The paper reports each estimate under four uncertainty specifications (baseline Wilson, annotation uncertainty, data-retrieval uncertainty, joint). The BASELINE (Wilson) point estimate is taken as the representative value because it is the observed proportion in the annotated corpus; the other three are re-estimations of the same quantity under simulation/bootstrap assumptions, not distinct estimates. Other specifications for this cell: annotation 19.7 [18.9-20.6]; retrieval 17.5 [13.9-21.2]; joint 19.8 [16.7-23.1]. VIEW-WEIGHTED SAMPLING - the single most important moderator here. The annotated sample was drawn with probability proportional to a post's view count, so the estimate is a visibility-weighted share of items, not a plain unweighted content share; the authors explicitly frame prevalence as "the proportion of the content that users are exposed to on the platform that contains mis/disinformation". Coded CONTENT rather than EXPOSURE because the denominator as reported is a count of POSTS drawn from a keyword-retrieved corpus, and there is no behavioural log or panel of actual people's consumption; an adjudicator who reads view-weighted sampling as an exposure estimand would move these rows to EXPOSURE (exposure_type proportion). Flagged rather than silently resolved. The value extracted here is the FIRST pair, the baseline estimate.

rob.design: Multi-platform, multilingual content study from the EU SIMODS project. Collection 17 March - 13 April 2025 from Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, TikTok, X/Twitter and YouTube in France, Poland, Slovakia and Spain, combining DSA data-access requests (only LinkedIn provided random samples) with keyword-based retrieval via native platform search or licensed third-party tools, tailored per platform (daily or biweekly searches, post-hoc date filtering, later engagement-metric updates). Corpus built from ~100 fact-checker-curated keywords per language over five domains (Russo-Ukrainian conflict, climate change, health including COVID-19, migration, local politics), ~50% neutral and ~50% ambiguous/misinformation-related; GPT-4o-mini assisted the manual filtering of off-topic posts. Annotation sample: view-weighted random sample (selection probability proportional to views) of 500 posts per platform per country, N = 3,000 per language; a Junior fact-checker coded all of them against a nine-label codebook, a Senior fact-checker independently coded a random 20% (600 per language), and disagreements in that subset were resolved by discussion. After dropping posts labelled Deleted: 2,947 French, 2,972 Polish, 2,976 Slovak, 2,940 Spanish (double-coded subsets 592, 592, 595, 581). No response-rate analogue and NO inter-coder reliability statistic is reported; instead annotator error is modelled with 3x3 transition matrices and 500 multinomial simulations, retrieval error with a two-level keyword/post bootstrap (500 x 500, keyword lists available only for TikTok, YouTube and X/Twitter), and both jointly at 100 x 100 x 100. Baseline intervals are Wilson score intervals. Ethics approval CE24-AA56 (Universitat Oberta de Catalunya); funded by the European Media and Information Fund; code and annotated dataset public at https://tinyurl.com/simods, keyword-to-content mapping withheld for platform-compliance reasons. Author-acknowledged limits: a single four-week window, four languages, six platforms, and prevalence sensitivity to keyword choice.
